newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-SWEDEN GO FOR GOLDEN DOUBLE OVER CANADA.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-SWEDEN GO FOR GOLDEN DOUBLE OVER CANADA.

text.p: Olympic champions Sweden are aiming to complete a golden double at Canada's expense when they clash in the world ice hockey championship final.
Game one of the best-of-three final is on Sunday with game two Tuesday and, if necessary, game three on Wednesday.

The Swedes, who were crowned Olympic champions after beating Canada in an overtime penalty shoot-out at Lillehammer in 1994, want to erase the memory of an embarassing sixth place finish at last year's tournament by lifting their first world title since 1992.

Canada will also not lack motivation as they try to end what has become an alarming string of second place finishes and begin re-establishing themselves as the sport's dominant force ahead of the Nagano Olympics next year.
Not only did Sweden deny Canada Olympic gold in 1994 but prevailed the last time the two met in a world championship final in 1991.
While Canada has won 20 world and Olympic titles it has claimed gold only once since 1961.
Canada are also still smarting from a last-second loss to the Czech Republic in last year's final in Vienna and a heartbreaking defeat to the United States in the inaugrual World Cup last September.
The Swedes, who trounced Canada 7-2 in round-robin play, are led offensively by Michael Nylander with five goals and nine points.
Defensively, the Swedes are rock solid, with three NHL players on their blueline, Calgary Flames Tommy Albelin, Los Angeles Kings Mattias Norstrom and San Jose Sharks Marcus Ragnarsson.
Behind them is New York Islander goaltender Tommy Salo, who was dazzling in a 1-0 win over the Czechs that propelled them into the final.
"We have to play a solid team game because Sweden is so well-balanced," assessed Canadian coach Andy Murray. "I don't see any weaknesses."
Sweden coach Kent Forsberg has spent the last few days cautioning his players and the media not to read too much into the team's convincing round-robin win.
"Our 7-2 win in Turku means nothing now," said Forsberg. "They're playing a different style now and they're stronger, having added Mark Recchi and Chris Pronger.
"Individually, player-for-player, they are by far the best team in this tournament."
With the exception of Dean Evason, Canada's squad is made up entirely of players from teams eliminated from the NHL playoffs.

Canada will be boosted by the return of the San Jose Sharks duo of Owen Nolan and Shean Donovan, back in the line-up after serving one-game suspensions for their part in a brawl at the end of the game against the Czechs on Wednesday.
Forsberg believes that in the end the gold medal will be decided by the team who can impose their style of play on their opponents.
The Canadian game, as always, is based on a strong work ethic with a hard-hitting approach that relies as much on pride as it does on skill.
In sharp contrast, the flashy Swedes will counter with speed and precision.
